newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-MISTER COOL MEETS THE CYCLIST.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-MISTER COOL MEETS THE CYCLIST.

text.p: Forget the flash cars, chunky jewellery and outrageous post match posturings that seem to go with the territory for some soccer coaches.
Saturday's Italian league match between leaders Juventus and cup finalists Vicenza will bring together two men who shun ostentation more than most.
Juventus coach Marcello Lippi and Vicenza's Francesco Guidolin are among the coolest in serie A and both took their current jobs three years ago.

Lippi, an elegant silver-haired 49-year-old with a resemblance to American film star Paul Newman, may rant in the dressing room -- occasionally lapsing into dialect for choice insults -- but his public persona is of studied calm.
As soon as a match is over, he heads for the quiet of home in his native Tuscany on the coast at Viareggio.
Whatever the result, Guidolin -- who shares with Lippi the fact that both were coaches at Atalanta -- is also a man of routine who can be counted on for two things.
First the 41-year-old will rattle off familiar cliches about keeping a sense of proportion, feet on the ground and never forgetting that Vicenza's aim is to avoid relegation.
He said that even when Vicenza led the league before Christmas for the first time in their 95-year history and he has shown few signs since of letting up on the theme.
When Bologna's plain-speaking coach Renzo Ulivieri said recently that he found Guidolin unpleasant and accused him of false modesty, the Vicenza boss steered clear.

"I don't get involved in controversy, particularly those started by people who make it a way of life. Personally, I see the job in very different terms: For me, respect for an adversary and all those in the sport comes first."
Lippi, asked for a comment on the spat, defended Ulivieri while adding: "I am for the quiet life, but also for clear speaking. I like it when people talk directly to me."
Secondly, Guidolin will get on his bike.
He is a cycling fanatic, a man who covered an estimated 10,000 kilometres on two wheels in 1996 and who would rather pedal to training sessions than drive.
"I get on my bike and I start to reflect, to imagine. I am alone with my thoughts and with nature," he once said.
He has also said that he needs the physical effort of cycling to stay mentally sharp and to "feel stronger at 40 than I was when I was 30 years old".
At the end of the season, Guidolin will probably be getting on his bike in a metaphorical sense as well.

With Lippi, he has been regularly voted among Italy's top coaches by his peers and is expected to be rewarded for Vicenza's remarkable performances under his guidance with the helm of one of several big clubs courting him.
Inter, who need to replace departing Englishman Roy Hodgson, are one club that has been mentioned along with Fiorentina, who have disappointed under Claudio Ranieri this season.

Sometimes called the anti-Lippi, mainly because his team have now beaten Lippi's twice in a row in the league and are one of just two clubs to beat Juventus in serie A this season, Guidolin is a tactical disciplinarian.
Lippi, who has had to be tactically flexible to accomodate injuries to various key players, has however achieved success on a scale that Guidolin can only dream of at Vicenza.

Sacked twice in his career -- at Siena and Cesena in his early days -- to Guidolin's once at Atalanta, Lippi has taken Juventus to the league title, the European Cup, the Intercontinental Cup and the European Supercup.
With Juventus five points clear of Sampdoria at the top of the league and the favourites to retain the European Cup, it is perhaps no wonder that Lippi can keep so calm.
